title: Common-Mode Response
intro: Real differential pairs are not perfectly balanced, and the tail source is not an ideal current source. Both turn common-mode signals into errors.

blocks.text: If Vin1 = Vin2 = Vcm and the tail source has output resistance RSS, then by symmetry each side behaves like a half-circuit with 2*RSS in its source:

A large tail resistance (a long-channel device or a cascode current source) reduces ACM. The common-mode input range is limited at the low end by the tail source staying saturated (Vcm >= VGS + Vov,tail) and at the high end by the input devices (Vcm <= VDD - RD*ISS/2 + VTH).
The most damaging effect is that a pure common-mode input produces a differential output when the two sides differ (gm1 != gm2 or RD1 != RD2). If gm differs by Delta-gm:

blocks.source:
A(CM->DM) = Delta-gm * RD / ( 1 + (gm1 + gm2)*RSS )
CMRR = ADM / A(CM->DM) = gm*(1 + 2*gm*RSS) / Delta-gm

blocks.text: CMRR (common-mode rejection ratio) tells how well the pair rejects interference: it is limited by the device mismatch and the tail impedance, so layout matching and a high-impedance tail both matter.

blocks.title: CMRR estimate
blocks.text: gm = 2 mS, RSS = 20 kohm, and a 1 percent mismatch Delta-gm/gm. Find the CMRR in dB.

blocks.title: Effect of the tail
blocks.text: If RSS is raised from 20 kohm to 200 kohm with the same gm and mismatch, what is the new CMRR?
solution: A tenfold bigger tail resistance gives about a tenfold better CMRR, 20 dB more.
